Hey! I'm entering the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1 "Touch Grass". The deadline is Sunday Oct 11, 11:59 PM PDT (2:59 AM ET Monday). DevRelay is connected. Use it to understand the challenge (rules, judging, prizes, submission template), and to study what people have submitted so far: what's crowded, what's missing, what tends to win. Nothing to build yet.

We'll run this like a real software company, waterfall style. I'll bring in one specialist at a time. I'll often send follow-ups through my manager session. Those messages come from me, so treat them the same as mine.

Each specialist:
- reads the earlier handoffs in docs/handoffs/
- owns their scope completely and decides how to do it
- finishes every deliverable in their role. No TODOs, TBDs, placeholders, or "next role will handle it."
- verifies their own work actually works, with proof (test output, screenshots, commands run)
- writes a handoff (docs/handoffs/NN-role.md) covering what was delivered, key decisions and why, and anything the next role must know
- commits their work with a clear message

Roles don't depend on later roles. If you find a problem from an earlier phase, fix it if it's small and log it. If it's big, write a change request in your handoff and propose the fix.

Ground rules for everyone:
- Research before deciding or debugging. Check how others solved it (DEV via DevRelay, official docs, GitHub issues). Keep docs/BUGLOG.md so nobody solves the same problem twice.
- Real, working output only, with proof. No mock data where real data exists.
- Secrets are already in .env, at <project>/flare/.env (if you're running in a worktree copy, read them from that path). They cover MongoDB Atlas, the Telegram bot, and RENDER_KEY for the Render API. Never print, log or commit them. .gitignore already protects .env.
- Anything public waits for my yes: deploying under my accounts, making the repo public, publishing, posting, uploading, or messaging people.
- Already approved, no need to ask: npm installs; installing Ollama with Homebrew and pulling gemma4:e4b; downloading the Gemma 4 E2B ONNX model (~3.2 GB) for browser tests; creating a private GitHub repo named flare on my account and pushing to it; keeping the Mac awake (caffeinate) during long work.
- A separate lab session is running technical spikes in lab/ (git-ignored). Don't edit or commit lab/. The engineering lead will review its reports and import what we keep.
- Real iPhone checks happen when we're awake. Build whatever page or script makes that quick, and we'll run it on our phones.

Writing rules, for every doc, UI string, commit message and the final post:
- Plain words, short sentences. Say the concrete thing: numbers, names, what happens.
- No buzzwords or filler. Don't use: seamless, leverage, robust, empower, unlock, elevate, delve, cutting-edge, revolutionize, game-changer, harness, synergy, holistic, paradigm, next-level, supercharge, effortless, ecosystem, tapestry, testament, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's not just X, it's Y", "let's dive in".
- No em-dash chains, no emoji decoration in docs, no intros or outros that say nothing.
- Every claim gets a number, a link, or proof. If we don't know, say so.
- UI copy is short and human: buttons 3 words max, messages 12 words max, warm and a bit playful, never cute at the cost of clarity.

Quality bar, for every role (product, design, engineering, AI, maps, PWA, QA, security, ops, docs):
- No timeboxes and no compromises. Take the time each role needs to do it properly, and don't cut scope to save time. The only fixed points are the Sunday daytime field test in Fairlane and the submission deadline.
- Each role produces the standard documents its discipline owns, at the level a strong company would expect.
- Use the latest stable versions of everything. Check current releases and known issues before choosing.
- Engineering work ships with tests, types, error handling and docs. No stubs, no fake data, no "works on my machine."
- The product has to feel premium: a full brand, polished motion and sound, and fast on every one of our phones.

Reply with your read of the challenge and the field, in 10 bullets or fewer.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: ~/.claude/skills/devrelay-challenges

# DEV Challenges & Events

The `devrelay-gateway` MCP server provides dedicated tools to query live DEV Challenges and community events directly from the DEV Events API (`/api/events`).

## Why This Exists

DEV regularly hosts technical challenges, hackathons, and open-source events (such as Hacktoberfest sprints and partner hackathons). To participate effectively, agents need access to the exact rules, judging rubrics, and sponsor requirements.

## Surface challenges without being asked

The user installed DevRelay partly so they stop finding out about a challenge the week
after it closed. You are the one who notices. Check `get_challenges` (and `get_events`
for livestreams and takeovers) on your own initiative when:

- The user describes what they are building, especially with a named framework,
  cloud provider, database, AI model, or sponsor's product.
- The user mentions a deadline, a demo, a submission, a prize, a hackathon, Global Hack
  Week, or a sponsor.
- The user is learning a technology or says they want to write more.
- A non-trivial piece of work reaches a good solve (see [[devrelay-publishing]]);
  the write-up may be an entry.
- The user asks what they should build or work on next.

Classify by date first (below). When an active or upcoming challenge fits, say so in one
or two lines: title, what it asks for, deadline with days remaining, link. Then offer to
audit the project against `full_details` and draft the entry. When nothing fits, say
nothing about challenges; do not pad a reply with irrelevant events.

For the user's own MLH hackathons, the same instinct applies through
`list_my_mlh_events`; see [[devrelay-offers]] and [[devrelay-mlh-submissions]].

DEV Events API features:

- **Event Type Filtering (`type_of`)**: Enables filtering events by type (`challenge`, `live_stream`, `takeover`, `other`).
- **The `full_details` Agent Context Attribute**: Added specifically to provide API consumers and AI agents with the complete, unabridged text dump of all event context (prompts, rules, judging rubrics, sponsor tracks, submission requirements, FAQs, prize tiers, and templates) that may not be displayed on the public event summary card.

## Choosing a Tool

| You need | Call |
| --- | --- |
| Active, upcoming, or past DEV Challenges | `get_challenges` |
| Full rules, rubric, and context for a challenge | `get_challenge_details` |
| Community events filtered by type (`live_stream`, `takeover`, `other`) | `get_events` |
| Full details for any specific event by ID | `get_event_by_id` |
| Stage/publish a challenge entry post | `create_article` (with `published: false`) |

---

## Working with `full_details`

When calling `get_challenge_details` or `get_event_by_id`, always inspect the `full_details` field. While `description` and `details` provide short marketing summaries, `full_details` is the authoritative source for:

1. **Submission Prompts & Themes**: What specific application, tool, or article the challenge is asking builders to create.
2. **Judging Rubrics & Scoring Criteria**: Explicit criteria judges use to score submissions (e.g. UX, code quality, technical execution, documentation).
3. **Required Tags**: Mandatory submission tags (e.g. `#devchallenge`, `#hacktoberfest`, sponsor tags).
4. **Sponsor Tracks & Prizes**: Specific category requirements (e.g. vector database integration, deployment targets) to qualify for sponsor prize tiers.
5. **Technical Constraints**: Requirements such as permissive open-source licensing (MIT/Apache 2.0), live demo URLs, or embedded architecture diagrams.
6. **Submission Deadlines**: Exact cut-off timestamps and timezone requirements.

---

## Temporal Awareness & Date Classification

The DEV Events API returns events from across history — past, ongoing, and upcoming. **You MUST evaluate `starts_at` and `ends_at` timestamps against the current date to contextually classify each event:**

| Status | Condition | Agent Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **🟢 Active / Ongoing** | `starts_at <= now <= ends_at` | Primary targets for current entry. Highlight submission deadline (`ends_at`) and days remaining. |
| **🔵 Upcoming** | `now < starts_at` | Announced events. Note start date; prepare ideas and dependencies ahead of kickoff. |
| **⚪ Past / Concluded** | `ends_at < now` | Submissions closed. **Never present as active.** Use exclusively for historical research, retrospective analysis, or winning architecture patterns. |

### Rules for Date Handling

1. **Never recommend entering a past challenge.** If a user asks "What challenges can I participate in?", filter out concluded events (`ends_at < now`) or explicitly group results by Active, Upcoming, and Concluded.
2. **State time remaining.** For active challenges, compute and report the remaining window (e.g. *"Active — 6 days left, closes Oct 15 at 23:59 UTC"*).
3. **Historical research context.** When using past challenges to extract rubric patterns or winning architectural designs, explicitly clarify that the challenge concluded in the past.

---

## End-to-End Challenge Workflow

Follow this 5-step workflow when helping a user participate in a DEV Challenge:

### Step 1: Discover Active Challenges

Call `get_challenges` to list active hackathons and challenges:

```json
{
  "name": "get_challenges",
  "arguments": { "page": 1, "per_page": 10 }
}
```

### Step 2: Fetch Rules and Rubrics

Call `get_challenge_details` with the chosen challenge ID to retrieve `full_details`:

```json
{
  "name": "get_challenge_details",
  "arguments": { "id": 101 }
}
```

Parse the `full_details` markdown for track guidelines, rubrics, and submission requirements.

### Step 3: Audit Project & Workspace

Audit the user's workspace against the criteria found in `full_details`:

- Check for a valid open-source license file (`LICENSE` / `LICENSE.md`).
- Ensure deployment configurations or templates (Docker, Railway, Vercel) are intact.
- Generate an architectural system diagram (Mermaid format is natively rendered on DEV).
- Validate required environment variables and setup documentation in `README.md`.

### Step 4: Draft the Submission Article

Draft a structured submission post following the template in `full_details`:

- Include an executive summary of what was built.
- Embed the architecture diagram and tech stack choices.
- Highlight how the project addresses specific sponsor tracks.
- Include links to the public GitHub repository and live demo.
- Stage to the user's drafts with `create_article`. Leave `ai_disclosure_level`
  unset: DevRelay sends `some_ai`, which is the honest level for an agent-drafted
  entry and what challenge rules expect (see [[devrelay-publishing]]):

```json
{
  "name": "create_article",
  "arguments": {
    "title": "My Project Submission: Building an AI Agent for DEV",
    "body_markdown": "...",
    "published": false,
    "tags": ["devchallenge", "hacktoberfest", "ai", "webdev"]
  }
}
```

### Step 5: Pre-Submission Review

Present a final checklist to the user verifying that all items from `full_details` have been met before they publish. Publishing is the user's call: set `published: true` only after an explicit yes in this session.

---

## General Rules Live in the Knowledge Base

`full_details` covers one challenge. The rules that recur across DEV Challenges
are in the `dev-challenges` knowledge guide (see [[devrelay-knowledge]]): the
Official Rules' eligibility (18+, excluded countries, DEV Members), teams of up
to four, the one-submission and new-work defaults, plagiarism consequences,
non-English entries, tie-breaks, and how prizes are paid. Where it and
`full_details` disagree, the challenge page wins for that challenge.

## Sourcing & Provenance

When reporting on challenges or events:

- Always cite the challenge title, event ID, dates, and canonical link (`location_url` or `https://dev.to/events/<id>`).
- If `full_details` is null or empty for an event, note that the organizer has not supplied an extended agent context dump and rely on `description`/`details`.

input.command:
cd "<tmp>/904c52d9-f200-4552-8ce5-05e400952efa/scratchpad" && cat > cats.py <<'EOF'
import json, re, sys, collections
arts = json.load(open("research/week1.json"))
# strict: week1 only by description/title or id after weekend cutoff
w1 = [a for a in arts if ("Week 1" in (a["description"] or "") or "Touch Grass" in (a["description"] or "") or a["id"] > 4803000)]
print("week1 strict:", len(w1), "ids", min(a["id"] for a in w1), max(a["id"] for a in w1))
cats = {
 "bird/birdcall": r"bird|birdnet|birder|avian|chirp",
 "plant/flora/garden": r"plant|flora|garden|botan|leaf|tree|mushroom|fung|forag|seed|crop|farm",
 "scavenger/quest/game": r"quest|scavenger|hunt|game|rpg|pokedex|pok[eé]|dex\b|monster|bingo|card",
 "walk/route/trail planner": r"walk|route|trail|hike|hiking|wander|stroll|trek|path",
 "screen-time/detox/lock": r"screen|detox|lock|offline you|close the|put (your|the) phone|stop using|ghost|unplug|laptop",
 "sky/stars/weather": r"star|sky|night|sunrise|sunset|cloud|weather|astro|moon",
 "run/fitness/sport": r"run\b|running|fitness|calorie|workout|football|sport|stride|cycling|bike",
 "journal/diary/notes": r"journal|diary|notes|log\b|memory|postcard",
 "audio/voice/sound": r"audio|voice|sound|ear|listen|podcast|song|music|whisper",
 "photo/camera/vision": r"photo|camera|lens|vision|picture|snap",
 "rocks/insects/wildlife": r"rock|insect|bug|butterfl|mosquito|wildlife|animal|wild",
}
c = collections.Counter(); 
for a in w1:
    t = (a["title"]+" "+(a["description"] or "")).lower()
    for k,p in cats.items():
        if re.search(p,t): c[k]+=1
for k,v in c.most_common(): print(f"{v:4d}  {k}")
tags = collections.Counter(t for a in w1 for t in a["tag_list"])
print(tags.most_common(30))
json.dump(w1, open("research/w1strict.json","w"))
EOF
python3 -I cats.py

            time.sleep(3*(attempt+1))

print("done")

# Challenge and field scan: Hacktoberfest Week 1 "Touch Grass"

Snapshot: Saturday 2026-10-10, about 16:30 UTC. About 37.5 hours before the deadline.

## The challenge

Source: DEV event 79, read through DevRelay `get_challenge_details`, plus the launch post and the HF26 hub.

- Launch post: https://dev.to/devteam/join-the-hacktoberfest-open-source-ai-challenge-week-1-touch-grass-2450-in-prizes-across-17-4pom
- Challenge page: https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05
- Hub with category rules: https://dev.to/challenges/hf26

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Prompt | Build something with open-source AI at its core that gets people off the screen and into the world. |
| Bar the organizers set | "The best builds here should make the screen the shortest part of the experience." |
| Bonus | Take it outside, use it, and tell us how it went. |
| Post must explain | Why open innovation matters for what you built, and where open beat closed. |
| Deadline | Sun Oct 11, 11:59 PM PDT = Mon Oct 12, 06:59 UTC = 2:59 AM ET. API `ends_at` is `2026-10-12T06:59:00Z`. |
| Required | A DEV post using the official template, tag `#hf26challenge`. New project built in the window (Oct 5 to Oct 11). One entry per person. Teams up to 4, one post, list teammates' DEV handles. |
| Later commits | Allowed only if noted in the README. Unnoted ones risk disqualification. |
| Judging | Writing Quality (weighted most), Relevance, Creativity, Technical Execution, Use of Partner Technology (optional). |
| Ties | Broken by positive reactions on the post. |
| Prizes | Overall $250 + DEV++ + badge. 6 featured categories at $200. 10 partner categories at $100. 17 winners. One win per person per challenge. |
| Agent session | Optional. "Judges love it." Save with DevRelay, embed with the `agent_session` tag. Uploads are unlisted by default, so make them public and scrub keys. |

A DEV staff member said in the launch post comments that people may submit by their own local time (comment 3ghbj, by heyitsjem). The official clock in the rules is the sponsor's. For us in ET, 06:59 UTC is later than local midnight anyway, so plan to the UTC time.

### Template sections, in order

1. Opening line: "This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass" (with the challenge link)
2. What I Built (what it does, how it gets people outside, who it's for)
3. Demo (deployed link or video)
4. Code (GitHub embed)
5. How I Built It (which open-source AI, and how the project is built around it)
6. Why Does Open Innovation Matter?
7. My Agent Session (optional)
8. Prize Categories (list each one, or remove)

Front matter tags in the template: `devchallenge, hf26challenge`.

### Category rules that matter to our stack

From the hub page:

- **Gemma ($200):** use Gemma, run it locally, fine-tune it, or serve it through Google Cloud or another provider.
- **Render ($200):** use Render as the AI runtime, host an agent's front end, or run Hermes or OpenClaw.
- **MongoDB Atlas ($100):** Atlas as the data layer, Atlas Vector Search for retrieval, agent memory, or the database behind an app on an open-weight model.
- **ElevenLabs ($100):** give an open-source agent a voice, transcribe audio for a local model, or narrate the demo.
- **Sentry Agent Tracing ($100):** show setup, latency, tokens, cost, what you found and how you debugged it, with traces or screenshots.
- **Entire ($100):** share the agent sessions behind the project in the write-up.

Partner credits (Render, Tinker, Backboard, ElevenLabs) are claimed at hacktoberfest.com/my/promos.

## The field

### Method

- Listed every `#hf26challenge` post with DevRelay `get_articles` (10 pages of 100). 947 posts in total. Dropped Weekend Challenge posts by tag, template line and ID range. **682 Week 1 entries remain.**
- Pulled the full text of all 682. DEV's API returns 429 after a few calls, so bodies came from the CDN-served article pages.
- Counted keywords across title and body. Counts are approximate: a word match is not proof of use, and the prompt's own examples ("bird call", "run club") inflate some themes. Theme counts below use title and description only, which is stricter.
- Reaction counts come from DEV API `GET /api/articles?tag=hf26challenge&top=7`.
- Two research passes read the top 15 Week 1 entries and all 17 Weekend winners in full. Their findings are in the last two sections.

### Volume

- 682 Week 1 entries with about 37 hours to go.
- DEV said the Weekend round "nearly tripled" its previous submission record (winners post, https://dev.to/devteam/congrats-to-the-hacktoberfest-weekend-challenge-build-for-a-friend-winners-pgc).
- Median post length 938 words. Middle half 628 to 1,285. Top 10% over 1,847.

### Themes, by title and description (n = 682)

| Theme | Entries | Share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Walk, trail or route planner | 169 | 25% |
| "AI that wants you to stop using it", screen-time framing | 155 | 23% |
| Quest, scavenger hunt or game | 124 | 18% |
| Plants, garden, foraging | 76 | 11% |
| Audio or voice | 62 | 9% |
| Wildlife, insects, rocks | 50 | 7% |
| Photo or camera | 43 | 6% |
| Birds and bird calls | 36 | 5% |
| Sky, stars, weather | 29 | 4% |
| Journal or diary | 28 | 4% |
| Running, fitness, sport | 15 | 2% |

Name collisions are heavy: TrailMate, TrailQuest, GrassQuest, WildQuest, TouchGrass, FieldNotes and close variants each appear several times.

### Models and runtimes (full text, n = 682)

| Signal | Entries | Share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mentions Gemma | 348 | 51% |
| Names Gemma 3 | 135 | 20% |
| Names Gemma 4 | 81 | 12% |
| Names Gemma 4 E2B or E4B | 39 | 6% |

| Hosted open-model APIs (Groq, OpenRouter, HF, AI Studio) | 85 | 12% |
| Closed APIs named (GPT, Claude, Gemini) | 40 | 6% |

Half the field runs the model on a laptop through Ollama. That conflicts with the organizers' own picture of a phone on a trail with no signal.

### Platform and features (full text)

| Claims offline or no-signal use | 439 | 64% |
| PWA or service worker | 111 | 16% |

| Native app (Flutter, React Native, Swift, Kotlin) | 17 | 2.5% |
| Telegram bot | 3 | 0.4% |
| Real-time group play (shared sessions, live location, multiplayer) | about 3 to 5 real cases (IRL Clash, Treasure Hunt, Touch Grass Bingo with shared card codes) | under 1% |

| Live demo URL (vercel.app, onrender.com, netlify.app, github.io, pages.dev, HF Space) | 265 | 39% |
| Video (YouTube, Loom, Vimeo) | 78 | 11% |
| Describes a real outdoor test | 66 | 10% |
| Embeds or links a DEV agent session | 27 | 4% |
| Mentions automated tests | 88 | 13% |

### Partner categories, by mentions in body text

content.text:
1. **The ask.** Build something with open-source AI at its core that gets people outside. The organizers' bar is that "the screen is the shortest part of the experience." The post has to say why open beat closed, and there are bonus points for using it outside and saying how it went. It's due Sun Oct 11 at 11:59 PM PDT, which is 06:59 UTC Monday in the API. Use the official template and the #hf26challenge tag. One entry each, and all code must be new since Oct 5; any commit after the deadline has to be noted in the README.

2. **Judging and prizes.** Writing Quality counts most, then Relevance, Creativity, Technical Execution and optional partner tech. There are 17 winners: $250 overall, six $200 categories (Render, TabPFN, Tinker, Arduino, DigitalOcean, Gemma) and ten $100 ones. One win per person. Reactions only break ties: the Weekend round's overall winner had 27, while some non-winners had 40 to 86.

3. **The field is big and samey.** There were 682 Week 1 entries as of midday Saturday ET, with a median post of 938 words. By title:
   - 25% are walk or trail planners
   - 23% use the "AI that wants you to stop using it" line
   - 18% are quests or scavenger hunts
   - 11% are about plants, 5% about birds

   Names repeat a lot: TrailMate, GrassQuest, WildQuest and TouchGrass each appear several times.

4. **Most entries don't match the organizers' picture.** About 51% run the model on a laptop through Ollama. 64% claim to work offline, but only 15% run a model in the browser, 4% run Gemma there, and 5 entries say they tested on an iPhone. Only about 10% describe a real outdoor test, 11% have a video and 39% have a live demo link.

5. **What's missing.**
   - Real-time group play in the same place: 3 to 5 real cases out of 682. [IRL Clash](https://dev.to/someshcoding/irl-clash-go-outside-take-a-shot-win-the-battle-592i) is the clearest.
   - Night use is in 4% of entries, haptics in 2%, custom sound in 7%.
   - Only 3 entries use Telegram.
   - Nobody tests with more than one person or over more than one walk.

6. **Partner crowding.** Gemma is the most crowded: 202 entries (30%) name the Gemma category. Render is next at 16%. The thin ones are MongoDB Atlas (27, 4%), Sentry (3%), Entire (7, 1%), DigitalOcean (1%) and Temporal (1%). Only 4% embed an agent session, and sharing sessions is the whole ask of the Entire category.

7. **What won last round.** I went through the 17 [Weekend winners](https://dev.to/devteam/congrats-to-the-hacktoberfest-weekend-challenge-build-for-a-friend-winners-pgc); 15 were read in full and 2 wouldn't load. They almost all had:
   - a named person with a real problem near the top
   - a table of measured results, and a "what broke" section with real bugs
   - a baseline comparison, even where their own model lost
   - code that owns the facts while the model only writes the words
   - one specific line per prize category, and a demo or video

   Length didn't matter: one winner was about 900 words. An entry that claimed 7 categories won 1.

8. **The bar for the categories our stack fits.**
   - **Render:** five Weekend winners hosted on Render, but only [Tala](https://dev.to/highcenburg/tala-free-audio-to-text-for-my-designer-friend-no-signup-no-credit-card-2o26) won the category. It ran the model inside the Render container, set up from a `render.yaml` Blueprint.
   - **Gemma:** [Kitchen Table](https://dev.to/uptimearchitect/gemma-4-reads-my-parents-mail-at-home-39-test-letters-9-of-them-real-and-one-calm-wrong-answer-3obf) tested e2b, e4b and 26b on 39 letters and let code override the model.
   - **MongoDB Atlas:** [Legacy Loom](https://dev.to/raphelevator/i-turned-my-sister-in-laws-voice-notes-into-a-cookbook-that-answers-in-her-voice-41ja) used Atlas for things it does best: streaming audio from GridFS to the exact second, and combining vector and text search.

9. **Risk for Gemma in an iPhone browser.** [Drift](https://dev.to/codeswithroh/i-built-an-ai-that-only-works-when-my-phone-is-in-my-pocket-3ipn) ran Gemma 4 E2B in iPhone Safari through MediaPipe, a 2.5 GB download. [Side Quest](https://dev.to/sizzlebop/i-built-an-ai-game-that-wants-you-to-go-outside-3a6k)'s iPhone 12 tab crashed about 500 MB into a 3.4 GB ONNX download. Our 3.2 GB ONNX plan needs an early real-iPhone test and a fallback.

10. **My read on where to aim.** The open space is a live, social outdoor experience that runs well on everyone's phone. It should be tested Sunday in Fairlane with several real people and written up as a story with a table of what happened. I'd stay out of trail planners and the "AI that wants you to stop using it" angle, and treat Gemma as table stakes rather than a reason to win.

The full scan, with method, tables and links to every entry cited, is in [docs/research/00-challenge-and-field.md](docs/research/00-challenge-and-field.md). It isn't committed, because there's no git repo yet. The counts come from keyword matches, so treat them as close, not exact.

Great scan, especially points 4, 7 and 9. One note on 6: we plan to embed this build session in the post through DevRelay, so Entire may be an honest fit. Keep that in mind, but don't chase it. Here's the founder brief.

Here's the idea, from first principles. People don't stay inside for lack of places to go. They stay in because asking is awkward, nobody wants to show up alone, plans die in the group chat, some friends can't use the spot, and phones die exactly where the good places are.

I want to build Flare: you snap where you are, and friends get a short invite. It only happens if enough of them privately say yes. Nobody ever sees a "no," and if it doesn't come together it shrinks instead of dying. Open-source AI runs on the phone. It should work for friends with disabilities and in places with no signal, and it should leave nothing behind. Being there together is the reward.

Less tech, more nature. The app should get out of the way fast. The place, the season, the light and the people are the point. A good session is about 5 seconds of screen and an hour outside.

We're shipping two things: the app (installable on iPhone) and a website that explains it.

My rough notes are in ../FLARE-SPEC.md. Treat them as founder input, not orders.

Facts:
- Testing in Dearborn, Michigan, near Fairlane Town Center, but it must work anywhere.
- Four of us (Fuego, Amor, Shilp, Ammo), all on iPhones (13, 16 Pro Max, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max). Two use Telegram, two use iMessage.
- No hardware.
- Sunday daytime to test it outside.

What I've learned about the field:
1. Gemma on Ollama is ordinary. Nearly everyone did it, so it won't set us apart.
2. On-device in the browser is the mark of the top entries (Side Quest, TrailSnack). We're doing that, plus the laptop fallback for the iPhone 13.
3. Nobody combined group coordination (quorum), privacy with a provable deletion audit, accessibility (talking compass, needs profile), and both a Telegram bot and links for iMessage/WhatsApp. That combination is our edge, not the model choice.
4. Fully open-source data storage (Postgres) isn't something any notable entry advertised, so it's a small extra point for the "why open" section.
5. Render is crowded as a category, and Gemma is very crowded. Our real target is the Overall prize.

Ask me anything you need, then we'll bring in the product manager.
</cross-session-message>

result.output:
1	# Flare: founder notes (v2)
2	
3	Rough notes from the founder. They are input, not orders. The team owns the decisions and can change anything here with a reason.
4	
5	**Challenge:** [DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1 "Touch Grass"](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05), tag `#hf26challenge`
6	**Deadline:** Sun Oct 11, 2026, 11:59 PM PDT (Mon Oct 12, 2:59 AM ET)
7	**Team:** 4 friends (Fuego, Amor, Shilp, Ammo). One builds; all four field-test.
8	**Test area:** Fairlane, Dearborn, Michigan (near Fairlane Town Center). The product must work anywhere.
9	**Phones:** all iPhones: 13, 16 Pro Max, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max. Two of us use Telegram, two use iMessage.
10	**Hardware:** none.
11	**Field test:** Sunday daytime, outdoors, the four of us.
12	
13	---
14	
15	## 1. What we're making
16	
17	People don't stay inside for lack of places to go. They stay in because asking is awkward, nobody wants to show up alone, plans die in the group chat, some friends can't use the spot, and phones lose signal exactly where the good places are.
18	
19	**Flare:** snap where you are, and your friends get a short invite. It only happens if enough of them privately say yes. Nobody ever sees a "no." If it doesn't come together, it shrinks instead of dying. Open-source AI runs on the phone. It works for friends with disabilities and in places with no signal, and it leaves nothing behind. Being there together is the reward.
20	
21	**Less tech, more nature.** The app should get out of the way fast. The place, the season, the light and the people are the point. A good session is about 5 seconds of screen and an hour outside.
22	
23	We are shipping two things: the **app** (installable web app for iPhone) and a **website** (what Flare is, how it works, privacy and accessibility statements, how to run it yourself).
24	
25	---
26	
27	## 2. States: fire words
28	
29	**Kindling → Lit → Ember → Gone**, plus **Sparks** (moments people choose to keep).
30	
31	- **Kindling:** the invite is out, and yes-taps are counted privately. Everyone sees only "need N more."
32	- **Lit:** enough people said yes. It stays lit once lit.
33	- **Ember:** it didn't light in time, so it shrinks: 15 minutes at the nearest bench, and one friend is enough.
34	- **Gone:** it expires and is deleted. Only a few counters and opt-in Sparks remain.
35	
36	---
37	
38	## 3. Two modes, one engine
39	
40	| | Flare (now) | Plan (later) |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| Start | Take a photo | "Sunday afternoon outside?" |
43	| Window | 60 minutes | Until a deadline, then the event |
44	| Shrinking | Spot → Ember at 30 min | A 4-step ladder (e.g. long trail → park loop → short walk → 20 min on the porch). Anyone can privately say "I'm fading," and it steps down. |
45	| Default quorum | 2 | 3 |
46	
47	**Conditions.** A yes can come with conditions in plain words: "only if Amor comes," "after 1," "back by 5," "just the short one." AI turns them into structured rules, reads them back to the person ("Got it: only with Amor, back by 5 PM. Right?"), and a solver finds the biggest group whose conditions all fit, at the highest step. Ties go to more people, then the higher step, then the earlier time. Free-text conditions never leave the phone; only the structured rule is sent.
48	
49	**Not lit.** Everyone gets the same "Not this time," so nobody learns who said no.
50	
51	---
52	
53	## 4. Ideas we liked
54	
55	- **Host line.** "Fuego is waiting at the bench by the pond." People go where someone is expecting them. The host can tap +1 for a friend who shows up without a phone. **Headcount** (host + arrivals) is the one metric.
56	- **Sparks and Hot spots.** After a Flare, each person who showed up can leave one line about the moment, in their own words and never AI-written. Later Flares at that place show "Your group has met here 4 times," plus one Spark. A Hot spots list shows where the group actually goes most. These are opt-in, tied to the place name rather than the exact pin, and encrypted with the group key.
57	- **Access line.** Every Flare shows what's mapped near the spot: benches, restrooms, water, steps. Each person's needs (avoid steps, max distance between rests, need a restroom) stay on their own phone. If a spot doesn't work for someone, their phone counts them in for the Ember instead, and nobody else learns why.
58	- **Talking compass.** Find your friend without staring at a map: "Fuego, 400 meters, slightly left." Arrow, distance and speech. It works with no map tiles and no signal. It helps you find a friend. It is not a mobility aid or an SOS device.
59	- **Spoken scene.** The invite photo comes with a short description that a screen reader can speak, for friends who can't see it.
60	- **Rest loop.** "Knee's bad, 40 minutes, want trees" becomes a walking loop that never goes too far between seats, with a large-print card you can print.
61	- **Fix the map.** On a walk you can photograph a bench or restroom that isn't on OpenStreetMap. AI drafts the tags, a person reviews every one, and it goes to OSM in a way that follows OSM's rules (Notes, or the user's own account).
62	- **Nature, gently.** One thing worth noticing at the spot (season, sunset time, the tree, the water), from real map data or the host's photo. Never invented.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## 5. Channels
67	
68	- **Link page (core).** Share into iMessage, WhatsApp or any chat. Friends open it in Safari with nothing to install and no account. The full experience lives here.
69	- **Telegram bot.** Posts the invite with live "need N more," gives private yes-taps, takes conditions by private message, sends "it's lit," and deletes its own posts when the Flare is gone. Members tap Start once.
70	- **Plain text for no signal.** Every Flare also fits in a short plain-text message (≤200 bytes), so it can go by SMS or iPhone satellite texting (iPhone 14 and newer in the US). Friends reply `IN <code>`.
71	- Mesh radios and door buttons are out (no hardware). They're fine to mention as "later."
72	
73	---
74	
75	## 6. No signal
76	
77	- Once a Flare or Plan is lit, everything needed (pin, compass target, loop, access line) is saved on every phone. The group can lock the plan, then walk out of coverage.
78	- On-device AI works offline after a one-time download on Wi-Fi.
79	- Nearby-places data is fetched live anywhere (OpenStreetMap) and cached. There's a ready pack for Fairlane.
80	- An outbox holds anything sent offline and delivers it when signal returns. Commits are idempotent.
81	
82	---
83	
84	## 7. AI (open models, on the phone first)
85	
86	| Job | Notes |
87	|---|---|
88	| Photo → invite (≤6 words) + spoken scene (≤20 words) | Gemma 4 E2B in the browser (Transformers.js, WebGPU) is the candidate. It's about 3.2 GB for image input, so the iPhone 13 (4 GB RAM) almost certainly can't run it. |
89	| Conditions → structured rules + read-back | Rule-based fallback for common phrases |
90	| Plan ladder from weather, sunset and nearby places | Deterministic fallback |
91	| Rest-loop request → constraints | Form fallback |
92	| Bench/restroom photo → OSM tags | Human reviews every tag |
93	
94	- **Fallbacks are required.** Every AI job needs a tier that works on every phone: on the phone, a laptop hub (Ollama with Gemma 4 E4B on our Mac), and a template/rules tier.
95	- **Report honestly** which tier ran.
96	- **Rules:** strict output validation, and never describe faces or identities.
97	- **Approved downloads:** Ollama + `gemma4:e4b`, and the Gemma 4 E2B ONNX model for browser tests.
98	
99	---
100	
101	## 8. Privacy promises
102	
103	- Photos are encrypted on the phone with a group key that lives in the link fragment and never reaches the server. The server only holds ciphertext, and only until Gone.
104	- Free-text conditions and needs profiles never leave the phone.
105	- Nobody's "no" is ever shown or stored beyond the solve.
106	- After Gone, only a few counters per group remain, plus opt-in encrypted Sparks.
107	- **Prove deletion.** A deletion audit after the field test shows zero leftover records. Put it in the post.
108	- **Be honest about limits:** Telegram sees what's posted in Telegram, small groups can sometimes guess who said yes, and SMS/satellite texts are outside our control.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## 9. Stack notes (the architect decides)
113	
114	- MongoDB Atlas, Telegram bot and Render credentials are already in `.env`. `RENDER_KEY` is the Render API key.
115	- I'd like storage to be open source too if it doesn't cost us much (Postgres, for example), because "fully open" is part of the story. MongoDB's TTL index is a neat way to guarantee deletion, and Atlas is also a partner prize category. Weigh it and write down the decision.
116	- License: something like AGPL, so anyone running a modified server has to publish it and the deletion promise stays checkable.
117	
118	---
119	
120	## 10. What I've learned about the field
121	
122	- Gemma on Ollama is ordinary. Nearly everyone did it, so it won't set us apart.
123	- On-device in the browser is the mark of the top entries. We're doing that, plus the laptop fallback for the iPhone 13.
124	- Nobody combined group coordination (quorum), privacy with a provable deletion audit, accessibility (talking compass, needs profile), and both a Telegram bot and links for iMessage. That combination is our edge, not the model choice.
125	- Fully open-source storage isn't something any notable entry advertised. It's a small extra point for "why open."
126	- Render and Gemma are crowded prize categories. The real target is the Overall prize.
127	- About 540 Touch Grass entries exist. Almost all are single-player (one AI, one person, one walk). Only a couple mention friends.
128	
129	---
130	
131	## 11. Data worth citing (checked Oct 10, 2026)
132	
133	- Face-to-face socializing for ages 15–24 fell from about 61 to 35 min/day between 2003 and 2025 (American Time Use Survey, via [Axios, Jul 2026](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/05/americans-socializing-decline)).
134	- Nearly half of young adults reported loneliness in an eight-country study ([WashU, Mar 2026](https://source.washu.edu/2026/03/nearly-half-of-young-adults-report-loneliness-in-eight-country-study/)).
135	- 68% of 18–34 year olds admit to flaking, and 45% have lied about why (UK poll: [IPA/Opinium](https://ipa.co.uk/news/flaking-data/)).
136	- 65% of Snapchatters' visits to new places are spots a friend visited in the past year ([Snap Newsroom, Jul 2026](https://newsroom.snap.com/location-sharing-redefining-friends-connect)). This is correlational.
137	- Benches along a route raised the share of mobility-impaired seniors (65–85) who would go outdoors from about 60% to 75% in a stated-choice study ([Netspar 2024](https://www.netspar.nl/en/knowledge-hub/do-modern-cities-encourage-or-discourage-walking-of-health-impaired-seniors/)).
138	- 12.2% of US adults have a mobility disability and 5.5% a vision disability ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/disability-and-health/articles-documents/disability-impacts-all-of-us-infographic.html)).
139	- Near Fairlane Town Center (3 km), OpenStreetMap had 54 benches, 6 restrooms, 2 drinking fountains and 24 parks on Oct 10.
140	- OpenStreetMap's Overpass API works if you send a User-Agent header. Some mirrors were failing on Oct 10.
141	
142	---
143	
144	## 12. Out of scope
145	
146	Accounts, passwords, feeds, followers, streaks, points, badges, "prove you went outside," AI-written itineraries, comments, ratings, a "No" button, money or prizes inside the product, mesh radios, hardware.
147

import math, datetime
lat, lon = 42.3087, -83.2166
d = datetime.date(2026,10,11)
N = d.timetuple().tm_yday
for kind in ("rise","set"):
    zen = 90.833
    lngHour = lon/15
    t = N + ((6 if kind=="rise" else 18) - lngHour)/24
    M = 0.9856*t - 3.289
    L = (M + 1.916*math.sin(math.radians(M)) + 0.020*math.sin(math.radians(2*M)) + 282.634) % 360
    RA = math.degrees(math.atan(0.91764*math.tan(math.radians(L)))) % 360
    RA = (RA + (math.floor(L/90)*90 - math.floor(RA/90)*90))/15
    sinDec = 0.39782*math.sin(math.radians(L)); cosDec = math.cos(math.asin(sinDec))
    cosH = (math.cos(math.radians(zen)) - sinDec*math.sin(math.radians(lat)))/(cosDec*math.cos(math.radians(lat)))
    H = (360 - math.degrees(math.acos(cosH))) if kind=="rise" else math.degrees(math.acos(cosH))
    H/=15
    T = H + RA - 0.06571*t - 6.622
    UT = (T - lngHour) % 24
    local = (UT - 4) % 24

# Challenge and field scan: Hacktoberfest Week 1 "Touch Grass"

Snapshot: Saturday 2026-10-10, entries published up to 16:46 UTC. The deadline is about 38 hours later.

## The challenge

Source: DEV event 79, read through DevRelay `get_challenge_details`, plus the launch post and the HF26 hub.

- Launch post: https://dev.to/devteam/join-the-hacktoberfest-open-source-ai-challenge-week-1-touch-grass-2450-in-prizes-across-17-4pom
- Challenge page: https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week1-2026-10-05
- Hub with category rules: https://dev.to/challenges/hf26

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Prompt | Build something with open-source AI at its core that gets people off the screen and into the world. |
| Bar the organizers set | "The best builds here should make the screen the shortest part of the experience." |
| Bonus | Take it outside, use it, and tell us how it went. |
| Post must explain | Why open innovation matters for what you built, and where open beat closed. |
| Deadline | Sun Oct 11, 11:59 PM PDT = Mon Oct 12, 06:59 UTC = 2:59 AM ET. API `ends_at` is `2026-10-12T06:59:00Z`. |
| Required | A DEV post using the official template, tag `#hf26challenge`. New project built in the window (Oct 5 to Oct 11). One entry per person. Teams up to 4, one post, list teammates' DEV handles. |
| Later commits | Allowed only if noted in the README. Unnoted ones risk disqualification. |
| Judging | Writing Quality (weighted most), Relevance, Creativity, Technical Execution, Use of Partner Technology (optional). |
| Ties | Broken by positive reactions on the post. |
| Prizes | Overall $250 + DEV++ + badge. 6 featured categories at $200. 10 partner categories at $100. 17 winners. One win per person per challenge. |
| Agent session | Optional. "Judges love it." Save with DevRelay, embed with the `agent_session` tag. Uploads are unlisted by default, so make them public and scrub keys. |

A DEV staff member said in the launch post comments that people may submit by their own local time (comment 3ghbj, by heyitsjem). The rules make the sponsor's clock official. For us in ET, 06:59 UTC is later than local midnight anyway, so plan to the UTC time.

### Template sections, in order

1. Opening line: "This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass" (with the challenge link)
2. What I Built (what it does, how it gets people outside, who it's for)
3. Demo (deployed link or video)
4. Code (GitHub embed)
5. How I Built It (which open-source AI, and how the project is built around it)
6. Why Does Open Innovation Matter?
7. My Agent Session (optional)
8. Prize Categories (list each one, or remove)

Front matter tags in the template: `devchallenge, hf26challenge`.

### Category rules that matter to our stack

From the hub page:

- **Gemma ($200):** use Gemma, run it locally, fine-tune it, or serve it through Google Cloud or another provider.
- **Render ($200):** use Render as the AI runtime, host an agent's front end, or run Hermes or OpenClaw.
- **MongoDB Atlas ($100):** Atlas as the data layer, Atlas Vector Search for retrieval, agent memory, or the database behind an app on an open-weight model.
- **Entire ($100):** share the agent sessions behind the project in the write-up, or search past agent work to explain why code exists.
- **ElevenLabs ($100):** give an open-source agent a voice, transcribe audio for a local model, or narrate the demo.
- **Sentry Agent Tracing ($100):** show setup, latency, tokens, cost, what you found and how you debugged it, with traces or screenshots.

Every entry is judged for every category it qualifies for. Partner credits (Render, Tinker, Backboard, ElevenLabs) are claimed at hacktoberfest.com/my/promos.

## The field

### Method

1. **Listing.** Merged three sources, because DEV's paged API skips and repeats posts as their order shifts (see BUG-001 in docs/BUGLOG.md):
   - DevRelay `get_articles` for the tag, 10 pages of 100
   - DevRelay `execute_dev_api_request` with `top`, 9 pages of 100
   - DEV's date-sorted search feed (`/search/feed_content`), which caps at 800 results per sort direction, run newest-first and oldest-first

   The union holds 2,009 `#hf26challenge` posts. Week 1 entries are those published from Oct 5 07:00 UTC on, without the `weekendchallenge` tag or the Weekend template line. **That leaves 813 entries.** All 48 most-reacted Week 1 posts are in the set. The only gap is Oct 5, 18:00 to 20:58 UTC, the first three hours after launch, which has 7 posts in the set.
2. **Text.** Pulled the article text of all 813 from the CDN-served pages, cut at the end of the article body, with HTML comments stripped (the template's comments mention DevRelay and agent sessions). On three spot checks the extracted text was within 1 to 7% of the original markdown's word count.
3. **Counting.** Counted keyword matches in the title and article text. A keyword match is not proof of use, and the prompt's own examples ("bird call", "run club") inflate some themes. Theme counts use titles only, which is stricter. Small counts (quorum, accessibility, Telegram) were checked by hand.
4. **Reactions.** From DEV API `GET /api/articles?tag=hf26challenge&top=7`.
5. **Reading.** Two research passes read the top 15 Week 1 entries and all 17 Weekend winners in full. Their findings are in the last two sections.

### Volume

- 813 Week 1 entries with about 38 hours to go.
- DEV said the Weekend round "nearly tripled" its previous submission record (winners post, https://dev.to/devteam/congrats-to-the-hacktoberfest-weekend-challenge-build-for-a-friend-winners-pgc).

Traits shared by the winners, ranked by how often they appear:

1. A named person and their problem in their own words, near the top.
2. A frank "what went wrong" section with concrete bugs.
3. Measured numbers, usually in a table.
4. An open-model argument tied to that person (privacy, cost, offline), not a generic one.
5. One specific line per claimed partner category.
6. Code-enforced guardrails: the model picks the words, code owns the facts.
7. A baseline comparison, including cases where their own model lost.
8. A live demo or video plus screenshots (all but one).

What didn't decide it: length (Viva won at about 900 words), reaction counts, numbers in the title (3 of 12), leftover template comments (2 winners had them), or how many categories were claimed (each entry won at most one).

Category bars:

- **Render:** the model or agent has to run on Render, not just the front end.
- **Gemma:** being there isn't enough, since 31% of the field names the category. The winner compared model sizes on a test set and let code check the output.
- **MongoDB Atlas:** Atlas has to do something only Atlas does well for the product (GridFS byte-range streaming, hybrid vector plus text search). One more database among seven claimed categories did not win.

| Founder claim | Finding |
| --- | --- |
| Gemma on Ollama is ordinary | Confirmed. 51% mention Gemma, 50% use Ollama. |
| On-device in the browser marks the top entries (Side Quest, TrailSnack) | Partly. 15% of all entries use an in-browser runtime, so it is common. Side Quest runs the model in a desktop browser that the phone pairs with; its iPhone 12 attempt crashed. TrailSnack keeps the 3.3 GB E2B tier opt-in and gated. Drift is the one entry that ran E2B in iPhone Safari (MediaPipe, 2.5 GB). Only 7 of 813 say they tested on an iPhone. The rare part is proof that it runs on real friends' iPhones. |
| Nobody combined quorum, provable deletion, accessibility, Telegram plus iMessage links | Confirmed, and each piece is rare on its own: quorum 0, deletion audit 0, disability-focused about 2, Telegram product 1, real-time group play about 3 to 5. |
| No notable entry advertised open-source storage (Postgres) | Not supported. 26 Week 1 entries (3%) mention Postgres or pgvector, and 3 Weekend winners used Postgres (Tala, Prep Buddy, Nivara). Separately, MongoDB's own FAQ says the SSPL "has not been approved by the OSI" (https://www.mongodb.com/legal/licensing/server-side-public-license/faq), and Atlas is a managed service. Postgres helps a "fully open" story; it doesn't set us apart. |
| Render is crowded, Gemma very crowded, aim for Overall | Agreed. Gemma 31%, Render 17%. |
| About 540 Touch Grass entries | 813 by Sat 16:46 UTC. |

Sunday timing: sunset in Dearborn on Oct 11 is about 6:57 PM EDT (NOAA algorithm at 42.31 N, 83.22 W). Sunrise is about 7:40 AM EDT.

# Bug log

One entry per problem we solved, so nobody solves it twice. Newest at the bottom.

Format: ID, date, area, symptom, cause, fix, proof.

---

## BUG-001: DEV listings miss and repeat posts

- **Date:** 2026-10-10
- **Area:** Research (DEV field scan)
- **Symptom:** Paging `#hf26challenge` with DevRelay `get_articles` (10 x 100) returned 947 unique posts. 24 of the 48 most-reacted Week 1 posts were missing. Paging `GET /api/articles?tag=...&top=8` (9 x 100) gave 701 unique out of 900 rows.
- **Cause:** The tag listing is ordered by a score that changes while you page, so posts shift between pages. The `top` listing has many ties at 0 reactions, with the same effect. DEV's date-sorted search feed is stable but stops at 800 results per sort direction.
- **Fix:** Use the union of all three: the search feed `https://dev.to/search/feed_content?per_page=100&page=N&tag_names%5B%5D=<tag>&sort_by=published_at&sort_direction=desc&class_name=Article`, the same feed with `sort_direction=asc`, and both API listings. Then check that the top-reacted posts are all present.
- **Proof:** The union held 2,009 posts and 813 Week 1 entries. All 48 top-reacted Week 1 posts were present. The only gap left is Oct 5, 18:00 to 20:58 UTC.

## BUG-002: DEV API rate limit makes bulk reads crawl

- **Date:** 2026-10-10
- **Area:** Research
- **Symptom:** `GET https://dev.to/api/articles/<user>/<slug>` returned 429 with `retry-after: 34` after a few calls. Throughput fell to about 5 articles a minute. `GET /api/articles/<id>` returned 404 for valid ids without an auth header.
- **Cause:** Anonymous rate limit on the API.
- **Fix:** Read article pages from the CDN (`https://dev.to/<user>/<slug>`). The body sits between `id="article-body"` and the first `below-post-bb` (or `id="comments"`). Strip HTML comments before counting words.
- **Proof:** 691 pages fetched in about 7 minutes at 0.25 s spacing with no 429s. On 3 articles, word counts were within 1 to 7% of the original markdown.

## BUG-003: Page-text extraction ran into comments and sidebars

- **Date:** 2026-10-10
- **Area:** Research
- **Symptom:** "Postgres" matched 332 of 682 entries, and the median post came out at 938 words.
- **Cause:** The first extractor looked for an end marker (`crayons-article__main`) that doesn't exist, then fell back to taking the rest of the page, including comments, sidebars and ad slots.
- **Fix:** End at `below-post-bb` (551 of 560 pages) or `id="comments"` (9 of 560).
- **Proof:** Postgres fell to 21 of 682 and the median to 725 words. Other counts moved by 2 points or less.

---
name: devto-research-method
description: How to list and bulk-read DEV challenge entries completely without hitting rate limits
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Listing: DEV's paged tag listing (DevRelay `get_articles`) and `GET /api/articles?tag=&top=` both skip and repeat posts while paging; one pass missed 24 of 48 top posts. DEV's search feed `https://dev.to/search/feed_content?per_page=100&page=N&tag_names%5B%5D=<tag>&sort_by=published_at&sort_direction=desc|asc&class_name=Article` is date-stable but caps at 800 per direction. Use the union of all of them, then check the top-reacted posts are present.

Reading: the anonymous API (`dev.to/api/articles/<user>/<slug>`) returns 429 (retry-after ~30 s) after a few calls. Article HTML pages come from the CDN with no limit; the body runs from `id="article-body"` to the first `below-post-bb` (or `id="comments"`). Strip HTML comments: the challenge template's comments mention DevRelay and agent sessions.

Details and proof are logged in the flare repo's docs/BUGLOG.md (BUG-001 to BUG-003).

**How to apply:** for any field scan of a DEV challenge tag. Related: [[flare-project]].

Corrected count: 813 Week 1 entries as of Sat 16:46 UTC (my first pass found 682; DEV's paging skips posts, logged as BUG-001). Median post 759 words. Other numbers moved 2 points or less.

On your 5 points:
1. Gemma on Ollama is ordinary: confirmed. 51% mention Gemma, 50% use Ollama.
2. In-browser on-device as the mark of top entries: partly. 15% of all entries run in the browser, so it's common. Side Quest runs on a desktop browser and its iPhone 12 tab crashed about 500 MB into a 3.4 GB ONNX download. TrailSnack keeps E2B (3.3 GB) opt-in behind a capability gate. Only Drift ran E2B in iPhone Safari, via MediaPipe at 2.5 GB. Just 7 of 813 say they tested on an iPhone. The rare thing is proof that it runs on real friends' iPhones.
3. The combination: confirmed, and each part is rare on its own. Quorum 0, deletion audit 0, built for disabilities about 2, Telegram product 1, real-time group play about 3 to 5.
4. Open-source storage as an extra point: not supported. 26 Week 1 entries mention Postgres or pgvector, and 3 Weekend winners used Postgres. Also, MongoDB's own FAQ says the SSPL "has not been approved by the OSI", so Atlas cuts against a "fully open" claim. That's for the architect to weigh.
5. Aim for Overall: agreed. Gemma is 31% of entries, Render 17%. Entire is noted as an honest fit if we embed the session.

Questions:
1. What time Sunday, and where do the four of you meet? Sunset in Dearborn is about 6:57 PM EDT. The test start time sets when the build has to be ready.
2. The test needs a public HTTPS link (a Render deploy) and the Telegram bot posting to your group. Both need your yes. Will you approve each one when it's ready, or approve now a private test deploy plus a bot that only posts to a group of the four of you?
3. Who publishes the DEV post, and do all four have DEV handles to credit? Is it OK to name Fuego, Amor, Shilp and Ammo, and show your faces or voices in the post and video?
4. Which iOS version is each phone on? WebGPU in Safari needs iOS 26, so this decides which AI tier each phone gets.
5. ../flare-plus.md, flare-money.md, persona-ideas.md, roundtable-ideas.md and orchestration/ are next to the spec. Should the PM read them, or does FLARE-SPEC v2 replace them?

The full scan, with a "Checks on the founder brief" section, is in flare/docs/research/00-challenge-and-field.md. Research bugs are in flare/docs/BUGLOG.md. Neither is committed yet, because the repo doesn't exist yet.

I checked your brief against the full field and sent the reply below to your manager session.

**A correction to my earlier numbers.** There are 813 Week 1 entries, not 682. DEV's listings skip posts while you page through them, so my first pass missed some. The median post is 759 words, not 938. Every other figure I gave moved by 2 points or less, and the conclusions don't change.

**Your five points:**
- **Gemma on Ollama is ordinary:** confirmed. 51% of entries mention Gemma and 50% use Ollama.
- **In-browser on-device marks the top entries:** only partly true. 15% of all entries run a model in the browser, so it's common.
  - Side Quest runs the model in a desktop browser. Its iPhone 12 tab crashed about 500 MB into the download.
  - TrailSnack makes the 3.3 GB Gemma 4 E2B model opt-in.
  - Drift is the only top entry that ran E2B in iPhone Safari.
  - Only 7 of 813 entries say they tested on an iPhone. Proof that it runs on our four iPhones is the rare part.
- **Nobody combined the pieces:** confirmed, and each piece is rare on its own:
  - quorum: 0 entries
  - deletion audit: 0
  - built for people with disabilities: about 2
  - an actual Telegram product: 1
  - real-time group play: about 3 to 5
- **Open-source storage as an extra point:** not supported. 26 entries mention Postgres and 3 Weekend winners used it. MongoDB's own FAQ also says its license "has not been approved by the OSI," so Atlas cuts against a "fully open" claim. The architect should weigh that.
- **Aim for Overall:** agreed. Gemma is in 31% of entries, Render in 17%. Entire fits honestly if we embed the build session.

**Questions:**
1. What time Sunday, and where do you meet? Sunset in Dearborn is about 6:57 PM EDT, and the start time sets when the build has to be ready.
2. The field test needs a public link (a Render deploy) and the Telegram bot posting to your group. Both need your yes. Do you want to approve each when it's ready, or approve now a private test deploy plus a bot limited to a group of the four of you?
3. Who publishes the DEV post, and do all four have DEV handles to credit? Is it OK to name Fuego, Amor, Shilp and Ammo, and show faces or voices in the post and video?
4. Which iOS version is each phone on? In-browser AI in Safari needs iOS 26, so this decides which AI tier each phone gets.
5. Should the PM also read `flare-plus.md`, `flare-money.md`, `persona-ideas.md`, `roundtable-ideas.md` and `orchestration/`, or does FLARE-SPEC v2 replace them?

I updated [docs/research/00-challenge-and-field.md](docs/research/00-challenge-and-field.md) with the 813-entry counts and a section checking the founder brief. I also started [docs/BUGLOG.md](docs/BUGLOG.md) with the three research bugs I hit. Nothing is committed yet because there's no repo.

Another Claude session sent a message:
<cross-session-message from="uds:<socket>" from-session="local_beb3cc8c-e162-46cc-bd0a-f870e8717ebd" from-name="Dev relay login" from-mode="prompting">
Thanks for checking the brief. On point 4, you're right: drop "open-source storage is rare," and let the architect weigh Postgres vs Atlas on the merits, including the SSPL point. On point 2, "proof it runs on our real iPhones" is the better framing, so use it.

Answers:
1. Test window is Sunday 11 AM to 3 PM ET, starting at a public spot near Fairlane Town Center. We'll confirm the exact meeting point Sunday morning. Plan for a release candidate ready by about 10 AM.
2. Ask me for each when it's ready. Until then, the bot may post only in our private "Flare test" group. Prepare both so each approval is one step for me.
3. I publish from my DEV account. Handles and consent get collected Sunday morning. Until then, assume first names only (Fuego, Amor, Shilp, Ammo), with no faces or voices unless each person says yes on the day.

Now let's bring in the product manager.

You're a senior product manager with 12 years shipping consumer social and mobile products, many under hackathon-style deadlines. Turn the founder brief into complete product requirements.

Deliver, all finished (docs/product/):
- Business requirements document (BRD): the problem, who has it, evidence with sources, goals, success metrics and how we measure them, constraints
- Market and competitive analysis of the existing entries (use DevRelay): what's crowded, what's missing, where Flare wins
- Product requirements document (PRD): problem, vision, target users, success metric, non-goals

- Risk register with mitigations

Keep the "less tech, more nature" line in every decision. When a feature adds screen time, it needs a strong reason.

Done = a team could build from these docs without asking you anything. Write the handoff for the analyst.

# Flare: Business requirements (BRD)

Owner: Product. Version 1.0, Sat 2026-10-10. Input: founder brief (FLARE-SPEC v2), field scan (docs/research/00-challenge-and-field.md).

## 1. The problem

People don't stay inside for lack of places to go. They stay in because of five small frictions:

1. **Asking is awkward.** A public "who's in?" invites a public "no".
2. **Nobody wants to show up alone.** Without proof others will come, the safe choice is to stay home.
3. **Plans die in the group chat.** "Maybe later" never turns into a time and a place.
4. **Some friends can't use the spot.** Steps, distance between seats, no restroom. They quietly opt out.
5. **Phones lose signal exactly where the good places are.** The plan can't be checked or changed once you're there.

Every existing "go outside" app treats this as a one-person motivation problem. It is a coordination problem.

## 2. Who has it

- Friend groups of 3 to 8 who already chat (iMessage, WhatsApp, Telegram) and meet less than they say they want to.
- Inside those groups: the friend who never commits first, the friend who can't see the photo, the friend whose knee decides the route, and the host who is tired of asking.
- Our test group: four friends in Dearborn, Michigan, all on iPhones (13, 16 Pro Max, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max). Two use Telegram, two use iMessage.

## 3. Evidence

| Claim | Number | Source | Checked |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Young adults flake on plans | 68% of UK 18 to 34 year olds admit flaking; 78% say they've been flaked on | IPA / Opinium, 13 Mar 2025, https://ipa.co.uk/news/flaking-data/ | Fetched Oct 10. The founder's "45% have lied about why" is **not** on this page (45% is "weather" as an acceptable reason). Do not use it. |
| Loneliness is common | "Nearly half" of young adults report loneliness in an eight-country study | WashU, 6 Mar 2026, https://source.washu.edu/2026/03/nearly-half-of-young-adults-report-loneliness-in-eight-country-study/ | Headline fetched Oct 10 |
| Friends drive where people go | 65% of Snapchatters' visits to new places are to spots a friend visited in the past year (correlational) | Snap Newsroom, https://newsroom.snap.com/location-sharing-redefining-friends-connect | Fetched Oct 10 |
| Benches decide who goes out | Benches along a route raise the chance a mobility-impaired senior goes for a walk from 60% to 75% (healthy peers: 90%) | Netspar, https://www.netspar.nl/en/knowledge-hub/do-modern-cities-encourage-or-discourage-walking-of-health-impaired-seniors/ | Fetched Oct 10 |
| Face-to-face time is falling | Ages 15 to 24: about 61 to 35 min/day, 2003 to 2025 (ATUS) | Axios, https://www.axios.com/2026/07/05/americans-socializing-decline | **Not re-verified** (site returned 403). Cite only with that caveat or find the ATUS table. |
| Disability is common | 12.2% of US adults have a mobility disability, 5.5% a vision disability | CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/disability-and-health/articles-documents/disability-impacts-all-of-us-infographic.html | **Not re-verified** (403). Same rule. |
| No-signal texting exists | iPhone 14 or later can send iMessage or SMS via satellite (iOS 18+) | Apple, https://support.apple.com/en-us/120930 | Fetched Oct 10 |
| In-browser GPU on iPhone | Safari 26 adds WebGPU | WebKit, https://webkit.org/blog/16993/news-from-wwdc25-web-technology-coming-this-fall-in-safari-26-beta/ | Fetched Oct 10 |
| The test area has places to sit | Within 3 km of Fairlane Town Center (42.3233, -83.2105): 48 benches, 9 picnic tables, 6 restrooms, 1 drinking fountain, 22 parks | OpenStreetMap via Overpass, queried Oct 10 | Our query. The founder's count (54, 6, 2, 24) used a different centre or tag set. Engineering re-runs it for the offline pack. |

## 4. Goals

| # | Goal | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| G1 | Four real friends meet outside on Sunday because of a Flare, with the screen used for seconds | Proves the product does its one job |
| G2 | Win the Overall prize of DEV Hacktoberfest Week 1 | Business goal of this weekend |
| G3 | Every AI job runs on open models, on the phone when the phone can, and reports which tier ran | Prompt relevance and "why open" |
| G4 | Nothing personal is left behind, and we can prove it | Privacy promise is a product feature |
| G5 | A friend with low vision and a friend with limited mobility can join as equals | Inclusion is part of "nobody is left out" |

## 5. Success metrics and how we measure them

Definitions are in 07-kpis.md. Targets apply to the Sunday field test (11 AM to 3 PM ET, four people, four iPhones).

| Metric | Target Sunday | How measured |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Headcount per Lit Flare | 4 of 4 on at least one Flare | Host's arrival taps, stored as one integer per Flare |
| Light rate | At least 2 Flares created; at least 1 Lit | Server counters: created, lit |
| Ember save rate | Reported as measured, with n. At least one Ember is triggered on purpose to test it | Server counters: embers, embers lit |
| Screen seconds, invitee | Median 10 s or less from notification to "I'm in" | On-device timer, sent as one bucketed number |
| Screen seconds, host | Median 15 s or less from open to sent | Same |
| Time outside together | At least 45 min on the longest Flare | Lit time to host's "Done" |
| On-device AI | Tier that ran is logged for every AI job; on-phone tier runs on every phone that passes the capability check | Tier counter per job |
| Deletion | Audit after Gone returns 0 Flare records, 0 photo blobs, 0 conditions | Audit script output, pasted in the post |
| Accessibility | The full invite, yes, and compass flow completes with VoiceOver on | Field test with VoiceOver on one phone |
| Post | Published on DEV with the template and #hf26challenge before Mon 06:59 UTC | DEV URL |

## 6. Constraints

- **Deadline:** DEV submission by Sun Oct 11, 11:59 PM PDT (Mon 06:59 UTC). Release candidate by Sun 10 AM ET. Field test Sun 11 AM to 3 PM ET. Sunset 6:57 PM EDT.
- **Rules:** new project built in the window; one entry; commits after the deadline noted in the README; DEV template; English for prize eligibility.
- **Devices:** four iPhones, iOS versions unknown until Sunday morning. Tiers are picked by runtime capability checks, never by model name.
- **No hardware.** No accounts or passwords for end users.
- **Open models only** for AI jobs. Gemma 4 E2B (browser) and Gemma 4 E4B (Ollama on our Mac) are approved downloads.
- **Approvals:** every public deploy, public repo, post, upload or message to people needs the founder's yes, one at a time. Until then the Telegram bot may post only in the private "Flare test" group.
- **People in the post:** first names only (Fuego, Amor, Shilp, Ammo). No faces or voices unless each person says yes on the day.
- **Writing:** plain words, numbers for every claim, the banned-word list, UI copy limits (buttons 3 words, messages 12 words).
- **Less tech, more nature:** any feature that adds screen time needs a written reason.

## 7. Out of scope (business)

Money, payments or prizes in the product; accounts and passwords; feeds, followers, streaks, points, badges, comments, ratings; a "No" button; "prove you went outside"; AI-written itineraries; mesh radios or any hardware; Wikimedia content.
